sentences.text: Kristjan was ten and lived in Tartu, which was the second city of Estonia — a small university town on the Emajõgi river in the south of the country.
His mother was a mathematician at the university.
His father worked at a hospital.
Every July, for two weeks, Kristjan took the bus north to Tallinn, the capital, to stay with his great-aunt Silvia.
Silvia was his mother's aunt — the elder sister of his mother's mother, who had died when Kristjan's mother was small.

Silvia was seventy-six and lived alone in a small apartment on the third floor of an old building on a cobblestoned street in the Vanalinn — the medieval Old Town of Tallinn, near the ruined church of Niguliste.
Silvia had been an archivist.
She had worked for forty years at the Estonian National Library, which sat on a hill just outside the Old Town.
She had retired eight years ago.

She was, most days now, a small careful old woman who took slow walks in the Old Town, drank strong black coffee, read three newspapers, and spent her afternoons at a large window with a view of the sea.

But two mornings a week she still walked up the hill to the library, unlocked a small back door with a key she had never given back, and spent three or four hours in the basement archive on projects nobody had asked her to do.
This was known to the current head of the archive, who liked Silvia, and who let her be.

On the first morning of his visit, Silvia gave Kristjan a small cup of strong coffee with hot milk — he was allowed only very weak coffee at home, so this was a treat — and a thick slice of dark rye bread with butter and honey.
She sat across from him and drank her own coffee black.
She said, "Kristjan.
This week I am going to take you into the library.
You are old enough now." Kristjan sat up straighter.
He had heard about Silvia's library work his whole life and had never been allowed to see it.
"I will show you the reading rooms," she said, "and then I will show you a small room in the basement that almost nobody sees.
And I will show you a project I have been keeping to myself for almost fifty years.
I have not talked about it to anyone in the family.
Now — well.
It is a good time." She drank her coffee.
She did not explain further.
They walked up the hill after breakfast.
The library was much bigger than Kristjan had imagined — a large pale stone building with many floors and many long windows.
Silvia took him in through a small side door, using a key from a ring she kept in her handbag.
She waved to a security guard, who nodded at her by name.

She led Kristjan through empty back corridors that smelled of paper and floor wax, past reading rooms where a few adults sat reading at long tables, and to a lift that opened only when Silvia used her key.
They rode it down.
In the basement, the corridor was warm and dim and quiet.
Silvia said, "The main archive is that way" — she pointed left — "and it is very big and very organized and cataloged by many people over many years.
Where we are going is a small room off to the side.
It is not cataloged.
It is what people used to call, before I was born, the 'strays cabinet.' Come." And she took him to a low green door at the end of the corridor and unlocked it with a small brass key from her ring.
The room was small and quiet.
Three walls of wooden shelves held perhaps fifty shallow wooden boxes and many leather-bound folders.
A single table with two chairs sat in the middle.
Silvia turned on the small brass reading lamp on the table.
She closed the door behind them.

"For a hundred and fifty years," she said, "the post office of Tallinn — and then the post offices across Estonia, when Tallinn was central — sent us here, to the library, the letters that could not be delivered.
Letters with unreadable addresses.
Letters with names of people who could not be found.
Letters posted after the person who wrote them had died.
Letters returned so many times the postmarks were unreadable.
The post office threw most such letters away.
But some — the older ones especially, the ones from before the wars, the ones that seemed to have some historical value — some, they sent to the library.
Because sometimes, a hundred years later, a letter about a bakery in 1885 becomes useful to a historian.
So we kept them.
In this room.
Nobody catalogs them.
There are perhaps eight thousand."
Silvia went to a shelf and took down one of the shallow wooden boxes.
She set it on the table between them.
She lifted the lid.
Inside, in a soft-edged neat stack, were perhaps a hundred and fifty envelopes.
They were pale brown with age.
The ink on them was faded to soft grey and rusty red.
She said, "This is one of the older boxes.
Everything in here is from before nineteen hundred.
Some from the eighteen-seventies.
Some later.
But nothing after eighteen ninety-nine.

I chose this box for you because it is old enough to be safely from a peaceful time." She said this last part with a small sideways look at Kristjan, and he understood that she meant, before the wars — before the terrible things happened in this country in the twentieth century.
He understood that Silvia was being kind by choosing this box.
"For fifty years," Silvia said, "since I was your mother's age and I first came to work at this library as a young woman, I have believed that some of these letters could still find their people.
That the descendants of the people they were meant for are still here, in Estonia, or elsewhere in the world.
That if you took the time to trace, you could find them.
I have believed this.
I have never actually tried.
Fifty years and I have never delivered a single letter.
Not one." She looked at him.
"I don't quite know why.
But I think we might try one this week.
If you are willing." And Kristjan, who was ten and slightly afraid of what he had just been handed, nodded, because he could not think of any reason to say no.
